code.python:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Done")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)

countdown(3)

prog.what: **Recursion** means a function **calls itself** to solve a smaller version of the same problem. To count down from 3, print 3, then count down from 2, and so on. Every recursive function needs a **base case**, the point where it stops calling itself.
prog.why: Some problems are made of smaller copies of themselves, such as countdowns, factorials and folders inside folders. Recursion lets you write them in a few clear lines.
steps: The function checks the base case first. When n is 0 it prints Done and stops.
If it is not the base case, it prints the current number.
Then it calls itself with a smaller number (n - 1), so it moves closer to the base case.
The first call starts the chain: 3, 2, 1, then Done.
mistakes: Forgetting the base case, so the function calls itself forever and the program crashes.
Calling itself with the same number instead of a smaller one.
practice: Change the start number to 5.
Write a recursive function that adds the numbers from 1 to n.
focus: dynamic
**Dynamic programming** starts with recursion and then **remembers** answers it already found so it does not repeat work. Learn the recursion idea below first.
backtrack
**Backtracking** tries a choice, and if it fails it goes back and tries another one. It is built on recursion like the example below.
divide
**Divide and conquer** splits a problem into smaller parts, solves each part, then joins the answers. Recursion solves each part.

prog.what: A **class** is a plan (blueprint) for making things of the same kind. A Dog class says every dog has a **name** and can **speak**. An **object** is one real dog made from that plan. The data inside an object is called its **attributes** and its actions are called **methods**.
prog.why: Classes keep related data and actions together, so big programs stay organized and you can make many objects without copying code.
steps: We write the class once. It is only the plan, so nothing runs yet.
The special first method (the **constructor**) runs when an object is created and saves the name inside it.
The speak method uses the saved name to print a message.
We create an object from the class and call its method with a dot.
mistakes: Forgetting the word that means this object (self in Python, this in JavaScript, C# and PHP).
Calling a method on the class instead of on an object you created.
Forgetting the brackets () when creating the object or calling the method.
practice: Change the name from Rex to your own name.
Create a second object with another name and call speak on it.
focus: constructor
A **constructor** is the special method that runs automatically when you create an object. Its job is to give the object its starting values.
inherit
**Inheritance** lets a new class reuse everything from another class and then add or change things. The example shows the basic class you build on.
polymorph|abstract|interface
**Polymorphism** means different classes can answer the same method name in their own way. Be comfortable with the basic class below first.
encapsul|access|propert|private
**Encapsulation** means protecting the data inside an object so it only changes in safe ways. It starts from the basic class below.
static
A **static** member belongs to the class itself, not to one object, so all objects share it.
struct|record|enum
This is a simple way to group data under one name. The class example shows the main idea.

prog.what: An **error** (or **exception**) happens when something goes wrong while the program runs, such as turning the text abc into a number. Normally the program stops. With **try and catch** you say: try this risky code, and if it fails, run this other code instead.
prog.why: Real users type wrong things and files go missing. Handling errors keeps your program running and lets you show a friendly message.
steps: The risky code goes inside the try block.
If it works, the catch block is skipped.
If it fails, the program jumps straight to the catch block (called except in Python).
The program then carries on normally after the block.
mistakes: Catching every error and printing nothing, which hides the real problem.
Putting too much code in the try block, so you cannot tell which line failed.
practice: Change abc to 123 and see that the catch block does not run.
Print a different message in the catch block.
focus: debug
**Debugging** means finding and fixing mistakes. Reading the error message and printing values are your two best tools. The example shows how an error is handled calmly.
test|assert
**Testing** means checking that your code gives the answer you expect. Handling errors, shown below, helps tests report problems clearly.
log
**Logging** means printing messages about what the program is doing so you can see where a problem happens.

prog.what: **Sorting** puts items in order, like numbers from smallest to biggest. **Searching** means finding an item in a list. Every language has a **built-in** way to sort, and you can also write your own with loops.
prog.why: Sorted data is easier to read and much faster to search. Apps sort scores, names and prices all the time.
steps: We make a list of three numbers in the wrong order.
We ask the language to sort the list.
The list is now 2, 4, 9 (smallest first).
We print the items one by one using their index.
mistakes: Forgetting that sort changes the original list.
In JavaScript, forgetting the compare function, so numbers are sorted like text (10 comes before 9).
practice: Add a fourth number and sort again.
Find the biggest number without sorting, using a loop.
focus: binary
**Binary search** finds an item in a **sorted** list by checking the middle and throwing away half each time. Learn sorting first, as shown below.
big-o
**Big-O** describes how the work grows when the list gets bigger. Sorting a list is a good way to see it.
bubble|merge|quick
This lesson is about one **method** of sorting. The built-in sort below gives the result you are aiming for.

prog.what: A **dictionary** (also called a **map** or **associative array**) stores **pairs**: a **key** and a **value**. The key is a label, like the name Ana, and the value is the data for it, like her age 20. You look up a value by its key.
prog.why: When you need to find things by name instead of by position, dictionaries are quick and easy to read.
steps: We create the dictionary with two pairs.
We look up Ana by her key and print 20.
We add a new pair for Cy.
We print how many pairs there are now: 3.
mistakes: Looking up a key that does not exist, which causes an error.
Mixing up capital letters, because Ana and ana are different keys.
practice: Add another person and print the size.
Change Ana's age to 21 and print it.
focus: hash
A **hash table** is how a dictionary works inside. It turns the key into a number so the value can be found very fast.

code.python:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(add(3, 4))
print(add(5, 7))

prog.what: A **function** is a named group of steps you can use again and again. It can take **inputs** called **parameters**, do some work, and **return** an answer. You define it once and then **call** it whenever you need it.
prog.why: Functions stop you from copying the same code many times. They make programs shorter and easier to fix.
steps: We define a function called add with two parameters, a and b.
Inside, return sends back the sum.
We call add(3, 4). The values 3 and 4 are the **arguments**.
The answer 7 comes back and is printed. The second call prints 12.
mistakes: Defining the function but never calling it.
Forgetting return, so no answer comes back.
Passing the arguments in the wrong order.
practice: Write multiply that returns a times b.
Write a function that takes a name and prints Hello and the name.
focus: default
A **default parameter** has a value ready to use when the caller does not give one.
lambda|closure|callback|higher
This idea builds on basic functions: a function can be stored in a variable and handed to other functions. Master the basic function below first.
scope
**Scope** is where a variable can be used. A variable made inside a function only exists inside it.
return
**return** sends an answer back to the caller. Without it the function gives back nothing useful.
parameter|argument
**Parameters** are the names in the function definition. **Arguments** are the real values you pass when you call it.

nums = [4, 9, 2]

total = 0

prog.what: An **array** (or **list**) keeps many values under one name, in order. Each value has a position number called an **index**, and counting starts at **0**. The first item is index 0 and the last item is the length minus 1.
prog.why: Instead of ten separate variables for ten scores, you keep them in one list and use a loop to work with all of them.
steps: We make a list with three numbers.
The item at index 0 is the first one, 4.
The length tells us there are 3 items.
A loop visits each item and adds it to a total, so the total is 15.
mistakes: Starting to count at 1 instead of 0.
Reading an index that does not exist, like index 3 in a list of 3 items.
practice: Add a fourth number and see the new total.
Find the biggest number using a loop.
focus: stack
A **stack** is a list where you add and remove only at the **end**, like a pile of plates (last in, first out). A normal list is where you start.
queue
A **queue** is a list where items leave from the **front**, like people waiting in line (first in, first out). A normal list is where you start.
set
A **set** is a collection with **no duplicates**. It starts from the same idea as a list.
tuple
A **tuple** is a list whose items **cannot be changed** after it is made.

code.python:
for i in range(1, 4):
    print("Round", i)

prog.what: A **loop** repeats code. A **for loop** is used when you know how many times to repeat. A **while loop** keeps going as long as its **condition** is true. Each run of the code is called one **iteration**.
prog.why: Computers are great at repeating. A loop lets you print 100 lines or add 1000 numbers with just a few lines.
steps: The loop starts with the counter i at 1.
Before each round it checks the condition i <= 3.
If true, it runs the code inside and prints the round number.
Then i goes up by 1 and the check happens again. When i becomes 4 the loop stops.
mistakes: A condition that never becomes false, which makes an infinite loop.
Being off by one: using < when you needed <=, or the other way around.
practice: Make it count to 5.
Add up the numbers 1 to 10 in a variable called total.
focus: while
A **while** loop checks the condition **before** every round, so it may run zero times.
do
A **do while** loop runs the code **first** and checks after, so it always runs at least once.
break|continue
**break** stops the loop immediately. **continue** skips the rest of this round and moves to the next one.
nested
A **nested loop** is a loop inside another loop. The inner loop finishes fully for every round of the outer loop.

prog.what: A **condition** is a question the computer answers with **true** or **false**, like score >= 70. An **if** statement runs its code only when the condition is true. Add **else if** for more questions and **else** for everything left over. The computer checks from top to bottom and stops at the first true one.
prog.why: Programs must make decisions: show a grade, check a password, decide if someone is an adult.
steps: We store the score 75.
The first check (score >= 90) is false, so it is skipped.
The second check (score >= 70) is true, so it prints B.
The else part is skipped because an earlier check already matched.
mistakes: Using one = (store) when you meant == (compare).
Putting the checks in the wrong order, so a high score matches a lower grade first.
practice: Change the score to 95, then to 50.
Add a check for 80 that prints a different letter.
focus: switch
A **switch** is a neat way to choose between many exact values. It does the same job as a long if / else if chain. Start with the if idea below.
ternary
The **ternary operator** is a short one-line if. Understand the normal if first.
compar|logic|boolean
Comparisons give **true or false**, and **and / or / not** join them. The example uses a condition you can change.
nested
**Nested** means an if inside another if. The inside check only happens when the outside one is true.

prog.what: A **string** is text, such as hello. It has a **length** (how many characters) and each **character** has an **index** starting at 0. Joining two strings together is called **concatenation**.
prog.why: Almost every program works with text: names, messages, passwords and web pages.
steps: We store the text hello.
Its length is 5.
The first character (index 0) is h.
We join hello and the text world together.
mistakes: Forgetting the quotes around text.
Adding a number to text without converting it first.
practice: Change the word to your name and check the length.
Print the last character.
focus: substring
A **substring** is a piece of a string, taken by start position and length.
format
**Formatting** means building a nice message by putting values into text.
regular|regex
**Regular expressions** are patterns for finding text. First be comfortable with plain strings.
split|replace
Splitting and replacing work on strings, so first get comfortable with the basics below.

code.python:
a = 7
b = 3
print(a + b)
print(a - b)
print(a * b)
print(a % b)

prog.what: **Operators** are symbols that work on values. The math operators are + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide) and % (the **remainder** after dividing). Multiplication and division happen **before** addition and subtraction, and **brackets** change the order.
prog.why: Totals, averages, discounts and scores are part of nearly every program.
steps: We store 7 in a and 3 in b.
a + b is 10.
a - b is 4 and a * b is 21.
a % b is the remainder of 7 divided by 3, which is 1.
mistakes: Forgetting that whole-number division drops the decimals in some languages.
Forgetting brackets, so the order of the math is not what you wanted.
practice: Change a and b to 20 and 6.
Check if a number is even using % 2.
focus: random
**Random** numbers make games unpredictable. Each language has its own tool for them, and they work with the math operators shown below.
increment
**++** adds 1 and **--** subtracts 1. They are shortcuts for the math below.
precedence
**Precedence** is the order operators run in. Use brackets when you are not sure.

prog.what: A **variable** is a name that stores a **value** so you can use it later. Think of a labeled box. Each value has a **type**, such as a whole number, a decimal number, text or true/false. A **constant** is like a variable that must never change.
prog.why: Variables let your program remember things such as names, scores and results.
steps: We create a variable name that holds the text Ana.
We create a variable age that holds the number 18.
We print both, so the output is Ana 18.
mistakes: Using a name before you create it.
Misspelling the variable name or using the wrong capital letters.
practice: Change the values to your own name and age.
Add a variable called city and print all three.
focus: constant
A **constant** holds a value that should never change, like a tax rate. Most languages have a special keyword for it.
type|convert
A **type** tells what kind of value a variable holds. Conversion changes one type into another.
pointer|reference|memory
This idea is about **how variables live in memory**. A variable is a named place in memory that holds a value.
comment
A **comment** is a note for people that the computer ignores.
input|output
**Input** is data going into the program and **output** is what it prints. The example shows output.
naming
Choose clear names with letters, digits and underscores, and never start a name with a digit.
